language_convention_note: 'Person with Tourette's' and 'Touretter' are both used in the community; the card uses person-first by default.
one_liner: Sudden, repeated movements or sounds that are hard to control, starting in childhood. Tourette's means both kinds for over a year.
in_simple_words: Tics are quick, repeated movements (blinking, head jerks, shrugging) or sounds (sniffing, throat clearing, words) that a person feels an urge to do and can only hold back for a while. They start in childhood, come and go, and worsen with stress, tiredness, or excitement. Tourette's means both motor and vocal tics for over a year. Tics are not deliberate, not a sign of anything 'wrong', and often ease by adulthood. Only a minority of people with Tourette's say rude words.
what_it_can_feel_like: It's like a sneeze. You can hold it, but it builds until you have to let it out.
People filmed my son in a shop. He was seven. Tourette's isn't a joke to the kids living it.
My tics are part of me. I'd rather people understood them than that I spent my life hiding them.
common_signs: Sudden, fast, repeated movements: blinking, grimacing, jerking, shrugging
Sudden sounds: sniffing, throat clearing, grunting, or words
An urge or itch-like feeling that builds before the tic
Tics that come and go, change over time, and worsen with stress
Starting before age 18, usually around five to seven
In Tourette's, both movement and sound tics for over a year

myths_vs_facts.fact: Swearing tics (coprolalia) affect only around one in ten people with Tourette's. Most tics are small movements and sounds.

myths_vs_facts.myth: People can stop tics if they really try.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Tics can be held back briefly, at a cost; the urge builds and the tics come out later. Suppressing all day is exhausting.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Tics are caused by bad parenting or attention-seeking.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Tic disorders are neurological and run in families. They have nothing to do with parenting or wanting attention.

how_common.plain: About 1 in every 160 children has Tourette's, counting those not yet diagnosed, and around 1 in 330 has a diagnosis. Simpler, temporary tics are much more common, affecting perhaps 1 in 5 children at some point.
how_common.figure: Tourette's: 1 in 162 children (0.6%) including undiagnosed; 1 in 333 (0.3%) diagnosed, CDC. Persistent tic disorders may affect about 1.4 million people in the US

what_helps.plain_summary: Many tics need no treatment beyond understanding and school awareness. When tics hurt, embarrass, or interfere, a behavioural therapy called CBIT (comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, built on habit reversal training) is the first choice. Medication can reduce tics when they are severe, prescribed and monitored by a specialist. Treating the ADHD, OCD, or anxiety that often come with tics usually helps most of all.
evidence_based_options: Psychoeducation for the child, family, and school
Medication for severe tics, prescribed and monitored by a specialist
Treatment of co-occurring ADHD, OCD, or anxiety
self_help_that_supports_care: Not drawing attention to tics; they fade when ignored and grow under scrutiny
Good sleep and lower stress, which reduce tics
A note for school: tic breaks, no penalties for noises, seating choices
Peer support with other families and adults with tics

when_to_reach_out: If a child's tics have lasted more than a few months, cause pain or embarrassment, or come with attention, mood, or obsessive problems, ask a doctor for a referral. Sudden, dramatic onset of tic-like movements in teens should also be assessed, as it can have other causes.
is_not: Fidgeting, habits like nail-biting, and the brief tics many young children have for a few weeks are not tic disorders. Repetitive movements that are rhythmic and soothing, like rocking, are stereotypies, a different thing. Compulsions in OCD are done on purpose to relieve anxiety, while tics are involuntary.
hope_note: Tics usually peak around age 10 to 12 and ease for most people by adulthood. Whether they fade or stay, people with Tourette's thrive in every walk of life.
strengths_and_differences: Many people with Tourette's describe quick reflexes, humour, creativity, and a deep sense of empathy for anyone who is different. The community is strong and often funny about itself, on its own terms.
in_young_people: Tics usually start around age five to seven and peak in the early teens. Schools can make a huge difference with simple adjustments. Bullying is common and should be addressed directly.
across_cultures: Tourette's exists worldwide with similar rates. In some communities tics are interpreted as spiritual or as bad behaviour, which can delay diagnosis. Awareness is improving thanks to advocacy by people with Tourette's.

sub_sections.title: Tourette's disorder
sub_sections.text: Multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic for more than a year, starting before 18.

sub_sections.title: Persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder
sub_sections.text: Either motor or vocal tics, not both, for more than a year.

sub_sections.title: Provisional tic disorder
sub_sections.text: Tics present for less than a year. Many children's tics resolve in this window.

sub_sections.title: Other specified and unspecified tic disorder
sub_sections.text: For tic patterns that don't fit the above, for example tics starting after 18.
